Free Trade As a General Rule

The idea of free trade comes out of Ricardo's work, demonstrating that even if a country is worse at doing everything than another country, free trade is still beneficial to both parties.

But, there is an implicit assumption in this argument that no longer applies. At the time Ricardo wrote there were more economically worthwhile things to do than there were resources to do them; production was constrained by resources rather than demand. That is no longer true. The industrial, and then the digital, and then the automation, revolutions have changed the playing field to the point where there is more labor in the world than is required to satisfy all the demand for labor while still satisfying all demand for economic output. What if a single country can satisfy all of the demand for goods of both countries in Ricardo's example?

When US jobs are sent offshore to take advantage of labor arbitrage (euphemistically called 'free trade') today, there are no better paying, more rewarding jobs to replace them, as economists believe, and would have us believe. Detroit remains an employment wasteland, while Mexico (Monterrey) gets the benefits of the exported jobs. Those jobs were mostly going away, anyhow, because of automation, but it illustrates the new world reality. Economists would have it that jobs spring from the land to replace lost jobs as a universal law, as inevitable as the tide. Because that used to be the case; it isn't any more.

In such a situation, does free trade still make sense? It will still ensure that maximum output is produced for the least cost to the owners of capital, but it will be contrary to national interests. To a country, it matters where jobs that produce economic output are located, while to an owner of capital, say a multinational, that isn't even on the radar; they care only about maximizing their returns. Maybe it makes more sense now to talk about reciprocal trade, where equal value is exchanged between countries, or worldwide trade in goods and services has to balance net - net.

Who's going to pay for all that redundant labor? This isn't the early industrial age when landowners just pushed their tenants off their land, and left them to shift for themselves. That redundant labor has political power, so someone is going to pay. Or are wealthy people going to have armies of slaves at their beck and call?

As industrial output increases without requiring additional labor, that labor can be redirected to the service sector. Much like as agriculture improved we shifted the vast numbers of agricultural workers to first industrial labor, then to the service sector.

TLDR: Technology is why we can afford to have more Youtube personalities and fewer farmers and hammer swingers while still increasing our standard of living.

I don't disagree with your assertion that technology frees labor. But your assertion that the service sector will provide is a faith based answer, an answer based on belief about a theory, the standard teaching of current economics. Where are all these service sector jobs in Detroit? Service jobs require someone who has earned wealth demanding a service. As wealth becomes more concentrated, because that's what automation does, rewarding capital at the expense of labor, can those with the wealth consume enough services to support all the labor made redundant? Will they?

I don't disagree with your TLDR, in fact it is STEM that generates all of our wealth beyond hunter gathering. But that says nothing about the distribution of that extra wealth, and the creation of jobs. I think you probably believe that new jobs will appear automatically because of 'human ingenuity', since that is the standard line taught in current economics. But that is just an observation, and can stop being true at any moment.

Any new jobs created are going to be in new industries. Because of automation, there will probably be a bifurcation; few highly skilled sophisticated jobs and more low skill jobs where people are used as programmable robots. To answer the concern about whether the service sector will grow, just look at the US over the past 50 years or so: manufacturing output has increased, manufacturing employment has fallen substantially, and service sector employment has grown dramatically.

I concur on the bifurcation of high skill jobs and low skill jobs as something which will increase, however I dont necessarily see it as a bad thing. Keep in mind that outside of luxury geographic areas (sorry bottom quintile people, it's time you wised up and moved out of SF, NYC, etc) the quality of life for people who're low skilled has increased dramatically over the past 50 years (discounting the anomalous bump from the post-WWII manufacturing boom in the US since everyone else had their industry bombed into oblivion). We just tend to ignore all of the amazing advancements as commonplace. Almost everyone in the industrialized world has clean, safe climate control in their residence, televisions, smartphones, the Internet, pricey but mind-bogglingly advanced medical technology, low barriers to income mobility (Poor? Go teach yourself to program on the internet for free), so much food there's an obesity epidemic, etc. All of that comes as a result of technological advancements. Despite those benefiting high skill people first (who can e.g. buy an early Tesla for $100k), that same technology becomes cheaper and more available. As an added bonus, much of that technology increases the income mobility of low skilled people. E.g. if you wanted to become a computer programer 30 years ago, the cost to acquire those skills was quite high. These days? A cheap laptop and an internet connection is all you need to acquire the skills to enter a high paying field.

Now the obvious question is "What about the people who lack the aptitude to acquire those skills?" That reminds me of back in history when almost everyone was illiterate. Did they "lack the aptitude" to learn to interpret complex symbols, apply arbitrary rules to them, and interpret the result by reading a book? Of course not. They lacked access to both a way to be instructed, access to books, and leisure time from their subsistence agriculture to acquire that skill. Which kind of reminds me of my example of why becoming e.g. a computer programmer is so much easier now. ;)
